As the 2026 MLB season comes to an end, with the Milwaukee Brewers crowned World Series champions for the first time in franchise history, discussions surrounding a potential lockout and the introduction of salary caps and floors have raised an important question: **To what extent does a team's payroll predict its success?**

This project aims to investigate the relationship between team payroll and regular-season success in Major League Baseball from 2021 to 2026, examining whether payroll can serve as a reliable predictor of a team's performance.

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
install.packages('baseballr')
install.packages("rvest")
install.packages("readxl")
install.packages('kableExtra')

```

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
library(baseballr)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(readxl)
library(kableExtra)



```

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}

# Create an empty list to store standings
standings_list <- list()

# Loop through each year
for (year in 2021:2026) {

  # Retrieve American League standings
  AL <- mlb_standings(
    season = year,
    league_id = 103
  )

  # Retrieve National League standings
  NL <- mlb_standings(
    season = year,
    league_id = 104
  )

  # Combine both leagues
  season_standings <- bind_rows(AL, NL)

  # Add the year as a variable
  season_standings$year <- year

  # Store the results
  standings_list[[as.character(year)]] <- season_standings
}

# Combine all seasons into one dataframe
mlb_standings_all <- bind_rows(standings_list)
```


```{r, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
excel_sheets("MLB Salaries.xlsx")

payroll_data <- bind_rows(
  lapply(2021:2026, function(year) {
    read_excel(
      "MLB Salaries.xlsx",
      sheet = as.character(year)
    )
  })
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
dim(payroll_data)

names(payroll_data)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
mlb_payroll <- payroll_data %>% 
               mutate(`difference in payroll` = `team payroll` - `last year payroll`)  %>%
               select(year, team, `team payroll`, w, l, `last year payroll`, `difference in payroll`) 

mlb_payroll
```

## Examining the Relationship Between Team Payroll and Regular-Season Performance (2021–2026)

To begin the analysis, we examine the relationship between team payroll and regular-season performance across Major League Baseball from 2021 to 2026. Specifically, we compare each team's annual payroll with its corresponding number of wins and losses.

Scatterplots are first used to visualize the direction and strength of these relationships. Pearson correlation coefficients are then calculated to quantify the linear associations between payroll and team performance, followed by coefficients of determination $R²$ to evaluate the proportion of variation in wins and losses explained by payroll in a simple linear model.

```{r, echo=FALSE,message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, out.width="85%", fig.align="center"}
# Payroll vs Wins
ggplot(mlb_payroll, aes(x = `team payroll`, y = w)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#264653",
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    color = "#E76F51",
    linewidth = 1.2,
    se = FALSE
  ) +
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
cor_win_payroll <- cor(mlb_payroll$w,mlb_payroll$`team payroll`)
cor_loss_payroll <- cor(mlb_payroll$l,mlb_payroll$`team payroll`)

rsqu_win_payroll <- cor(mlb_payroll$w,mlb_payroll$`team payroll`)^2
rsqu_loss_payroll <- cor(mlb_payroll$l,mlb_payroll$`team payroll`)^2

correlation_table <- data.frame(
  Relationship = c("Payroll vs. Wins", "Payroll vs. Losses"),
  Correlation = c(cor_win_payroll, cor_loss_payroll),
  R_Squared = c(rsqu_win_payroll, rsqu_loss_payroll)
)

correlation_table %>%
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    col.names = c("Relationship", "Pearson's r", "R²"),
    caption = "Relationship Between MLB Team Payroll and Regular-Season Performance (2021–2026)",
    align = c("l", "c", "c"),
    booktabs = TRUE
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )
```

The relationship between team payroll and regular-season wins is positive, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.3417, indicating a weak-to-moderate linear association. An R-squared value of 0.1168 suggests that approximately 11.68% of the variation in team wins is explained by payroll in the simple linear model.

Conversely, the relationship between payroll and losses is negative, with a correlation coefficient of −0.3431. The corresponding R-squared value of 0.1177 indicates that approximately 11.77% of the variation in losses is explained by payroll.

Overall, these results suggest that while higher payrolls are generally associated with more wins and fewer losses, payroll alone explains a relatively small proportion of the variation in regular-season performance.

## Examining the Relationship Between Year-Over-Year Changes in Team Payroll and Regular-Season Performance (2021–2026)

While the previous section examined the relationship between total team payroll and regular-season performance, this section investigates whether changes in payroll are associated with changes in team success from one season to the next.

To examine this relationship, we calculated the year-over-year differences in team payroll, wins, and losses. For each organization, the previous season's value was subtracted from the current season's value, allowing us to examine whether increases or decreases in spending corresponded with improvements or declines in regular-season performance.


$$
\Delta P_{it} = P_{it} - P_{i,t-1}
$$

$$
\Delta W_{it} = W_{it} - W_{i,t-1}
$$

$$
\Delta L_{it} = L_{it} - L_{i,t-1}
$$


Because the dataset covers the 2021–2026 seasons, year-over-year comparisons were conducted from 2022 to 2026, resulting in 150 potential team-season comparisons.

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
payroll_data_2 <- payroll_data %>% group_by(team) %>%
                  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
                  mutate(wins_change = w - lag(w)) %>%
                  ungroup()

payroll_data_2 <- payroll_data_2 %>% group_by(team) %>%
                  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
                  mutate(losses_change = l - lag(l)) %>%
                  ungroup()

payroll_data_2 <- payroll_data_2 %>% group_by(team) %>%
                  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
                  mutate(payroll_change = `team payroll` - lag(`team payroll`)) %>%
                  ungroup()
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
payroll_data_2 <- payroll_data_2 %>%
  tidyr::drop_na(wins_change, losses_change, payroll_change)
```

The relationship between year-over-year changes in team payroll and changes in regular-season performance appears to be extremely weak.

The correlation between changes in payroll and wins was -0.0759, indicating a very weak negative relationship. An R-squared value of 0.00576 suggests that approximately 0.58% of the variation in year-over-year changes in wins can be explained by changes in team payroll.

Conversely, the correlation between changes in payroll and losses was 0.0781, indicating a very weak positive relationship. The corresponding R-squared value of 0.00611 indicates that approximately 0.61% of the variation in changes in losses can be explained by changes in payroll.

Overall, these findings suggest that increases or decreases in team payroll have little linear association with improvements or declines in regular-season performance. While changes in spending may influence individual teams, the results indicate that payroll changes alone are not reliable predictors of year-over-year changes in wins or losses across Major League Baseball.

## Developing and Evaluating a Payroll Efficiency Metric in Major League Baseball

To further investigate the relationship between team payroll and regular-season performance, this section will introduce a measure of payroll efficiency. The objective is to determine whether MLB organizations are receiving sufficient value from their financial investments in player salaries.

### Initial Measure: Cost per Win

To begin our analysis of payroll efficiency, we developed a simple cost-per-win metric that measures the amount of money an MLB organization spends in player payroll for each regular-season victory.

The metric is calculated as follows:

$$
\text{Cost per Win}_{it} = \frac{P_{it}}{W_{it}}
$$

Where:

$P_{it}$ represents team $i's$ total payroll in season $t$.

$W_{it}$ represents the number of regular-season wins achieved by team $i$ in season $t$.

Under this calculation, a lower value indicates that a team spends fewer dollars per victory. However, this metric does not independently account for competitive success, meaning that teams with low payrolls can rank highly despite finishing with losing records.

```{r,, echo = FALSE}
payroll_data_3 <- payroll_data %>% mutate(dollars_per_win = `team payroll`/w) %>% 
                  arrange((dollars_per_win))

# Create formatted top 5 table
payroll_data_3 %>%
  filter(year == 2026) %>%
  arrange(dollars_per_win) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  mutate(
    Rank = row_number(),
    dollars_per_win = scales::dollar(
      dollars_per_win,
      accuracy = 1
    )
  ) %>%
  select(Rank, team, year, w, dollars_per_win) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Rank", "Team", "Year", "Wins", "Cost per Win"
    ),
    caption = "Top 5 MLB Teams by Lowest Cost per Win (2026)",
    align = c("c", "l", "c", "c", "r"),
    booktabs = TRUE
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )
```
The initial cost-per-win analysis revealed that the Milwaukee Brewers ranked among the five most financially efficient teams in 2026. With 103 regular-season wins, the Brewers spent approximately 1,349,518 dollars per victory. However, the Miami Marlins ranked first, spending approximately 1,024,268 dollars per win.

Miami's ranking highlights a limitation of using cost per win as the sole measure of payroll efficiency. Despite finishing with only 80 wins, two games below a .500 winning percentage, the Marlins were technically the most financially efficient team in baseball under this metric. This raises an important question: should a team be considered financially efficient simply because it spends relatively little, even if it fails to achieve a winning record?

### Revised Measure: Payroll Efficiency Index

To address the limitations of the initial cost-per-win metric, we developed a revised efficiency index that incorporates team performance relative to the league average.

First, we calculated the average number of regular-season wins across all MLB team-season observations from 2021 to 2026:

$$
\overline{W}=\frac{\sum_{i,t}W_{it}}{N}
$$

Where $N$ represents the total number of team-season observations in the dataset.

Using this baseline, we constructed the following payroll efficiency index:

$$
E_{it}=\frac{W_{it}-\overline{W}}{P_{it}/1{,}000{,}000}
$$

Where:

Where:

- $E_{it}$ represents the payroll efficiency score for team $i$ in season $t$.
- $W_{it}$ represents team $i$'s regular-season wins in season $t$.
- $\overline{W}$ represents the average number of regular-season wins across all MLB teams from 2021 to 2026.
- $P_{it}$ represents team $i$'s total payroll in US dollars for season $t$.
- $i$ represents the individual MLB team.
- $t$ represents the season being analyzed.

This index measures the number of wins above league average achieved per $1 million in team payroll. A positive score indicates above-average regular-season performance, while a negative score indicates below-average performance. Higher scores represent greater payroll-adjusted success under this metric.

Unlike the original cost-per-win calculation, the revised index distinguishes teams that achieve winning results from those that spend relatively little but perform below league average.

```{r, echo = FALSE, include=FALSE}
payroll_data_3B <- payroll_data %>% mutate(efficancy_score = (w -                                             mean(w))/(`team payroll`/1000000))

payroll_data_3B %>%
  filter(year == 2026) %>%
  arrange(desc(efficancy_score)) %>%
  select(team, year, w, efficancy_score) %>%
  head(5)
```




### Evaluating Long-Term Payroll Efficiency
While individual-season efficiency scores provide insight into annual performance, they do not necessarily reflect an organization's ability to sustain payroll efficiency over time.

To investigate long-term performance, we calculated the arithmetic mean of each team's annual efficiency scores from 2021 to 2026:

$$
\overline{E}i=\frac{1}{6}\sum{t=2021}^{2026}E_{it}
$$

Where $(\overline{E}_i)$ represents team $(i)'s$ average annual efficiency score over the six seasons.

This calculation assigns equal weight to each season, allowing us to compare organizations based on their average payroll-adjusted performance rather than relying on a single exceptional year.

However, because this approach averages annual ratios, it does not necessarily produce the same rankings as dividing total wins above average by total payroll across the six seasons. This distinction will be examined in the subsequent sensitivity analysis.
\newpage
```{r, echo = FALSE}
annual_top_5 <- payroll_data_3B %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  arrange(desc(efficancy_score), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(year, rank, team, w, efficancy_score)

knitr::kable(
  annual_top_5,
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c("Year", "Rank", "Team", "Wins", "Efficiency Score"),
  caption = "Top 5 MLB Teams by Payroll Efficiency, 2021–2026",
  booktabs = TRUE
) %>%
  kableExtra::row_spec(
    c(5, 10, 15, 20, 25),
    hline_after = TRUE
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = "hold_position",
    full_width = FALSE
  )
```

Examining the annual payroll efficiency rankings from 2021 to 2026 reveals several interesting patterns. Most notably, the Milwaukee Brewers ranked among the five most efficient teams in five of the six seasons analyzed, suggesting a consistent ability to achieve above-average regular-season success relative to their payroll. Similarly, the Tampa Bay Rays frequently appeared near the top of the rankings, indicating that they have also consistently performed well relative to their financial resources.

Another notable observation is the consistent presence of the Los Angeles Dodgers among the five most efficient teams. Unlike the Brewers and Rays, the Dodgers have operated with substantially larger payrolls, frequently ranking among MLB's highest-spending organizations. Their strong efficiency rankings demonstrate that high spending does not necessarily prevent a team from achieving favourable payroll-adjusted results. This contrasts with the New York Mets, another organization known for its substantial payroll, which did not appear among the annual top-five rankings presented. This difference suggests that financial resources alone do not guarantee efficient regular-season performance.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
average_efficiency <- payroll_data_3B %>%
  group_by(team) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_efficiency = mean(efficancy_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_efficiency))

# Create top 10 table
average_efficiency %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  mutate(
    Rank = row_number(),
    avg_efficiency = round(avg_efficiency, 4)
  ) %>%
  select(Rank, team, avg_efficiency) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Rank", "Team", "Average Efficiency Score"),
    caption = "Top 10 MLB Teams by Average Payroll Efficiency (2021–2026)",
    align = c("c", "l", "r"),
    booktabs = TRUE,
    digits = 4
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )
```


When comparing average efficiency scores across the entire 2021–2026 period, the Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers emerge as the two highest-ranked organizations, with average scores of 0.1220 and 0.1180, respectively. There is then a noticeable decline to the Los Angeles Dodgers (0.0756) and Cleveland Guardians (0.0702), followed by another decrease to the Atlanta Braves (0.0585) and the remaining teams.

Overall, these findings suggest that certain MLB organizations have demonstrated a sustained ability to achieve above-average regular-season results relative to their payroll. While the Brewers and Rays stand out for their consistently strong efficiency scores, the Dodgers demonstrate that organizations with substantial financial resources can also perform efficiently under this metric. However, these rankings depend on the definition of payroll efficiency used and should not be interpreted as definitive measures of organizational effectiveness.
